segments.t: Armed with a kitchen knife just in case, Senya and Fedya creep out to the courtyard to scare the photographer sitting in a car outside the restaurant. The plan goes horribly wrong when Fedya panics during the confrontation and accidentally knocks the man out cold.
Если тебе хлеба вдруг внезапно нужно будет нарезать?
Давай, ты иди, я на шутку поставлю.
Слушай, зачем же я пошёл с тобой?
Right, let's take their exchange slowly and unpack the Russian.
'We will just scare him a little, right?' In Russian, the idea of 'just' flows naturally into 'yes' without extra filler words.
'What do you need this knife for?' In everyday Russian, 'what for' flows straight into 'knife' without extra linking words.
'Just in case.' Spoken Russian keeps this brisk, leaning on 'on' and finishing on 'case'. Nastya answers right away.
Если тебе хлеба вдруг внезапно нужно будет нарезать?
'In case you suddenly need to slice some bread?' Nastya addresses the listener with the informal singular 'you' alongside 'to slice'.
'We agreed we are only going to scare him.' Kostya anchors the line on 'to finish speaking', while 'we'll scare a little' completes the thought.
Давай, ты иди, я на шутку поставлю.
'Go on, you go ahead and I will keep watch.' Nastya addresses the listener with the informal singular 'you' alongside 'will set'. Kostya answers right away.
'It is nothing, come on, get going.' Kostya anchors the line on 'yes', while 'let's' completes the thought.
'Guys, what on earth is going on?' Nastya brings out the contrast between 'kids' and 'what' in a few short words.
'Keep quiet, keep quiet, hush!' Notice how Russian expresses 'easy' and 'you' with crisp inflection rather than helper words. Nastya answers right away.
'What have you done?' In spoken Russian, the words stay in their normal statement order and Nastya's rising voice at the end turns the line into a question.
'I just wanted to scare him a little.' Here the Russian phrasing highlights 'to scare a little' before landing on 'a little'.
'Why did you even touch him at all?' The grammar packs 'you' and 'at all' into a tight, idiomatic kitchen exchange. Kostya answers right away.
Слушай, зачем же я пошёл с тобой?

'Listen, why on earth did I go with you?' Here Kostya anchors the thought on 'listen' and finishes on 'went, set off', keeping the spoken rhythm brisk and natural. Now let's listen to the entire scene again without interruption.

Давай, ты иди, я на шутку поставлю.

That wraps up this scene as senya and Fedya sneak out to intimidate the man sitting in a parked car outside Claude Monet, but Fedya accidentally knocks him unconscious. See you next time!
